575.title: Lift up your heads (Luke 21:5–28)
575.hook: wars and signs; but when these things begin, look up
575.howItsDone: Many churches read Jesus's words about the end in the season of Advent, when Christians prepare both for Christmas and for Christ's return, and they pray in the creeds that he will come again.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a widow's two lepta, more than they all. Your line was out of her poverty.

Some people in the temple courts are admiring the building, and it deserved it: huge pale stones, gifts hung on the walls, a sanctuary still being finished and enlarged after decades of work. Jesus looks at the same walls and says the days are coming when not one stone will be left upon another. His friends want details. When? What sign? He doesn't give a date. He gives a long list of frightening things, and then an instruction about where to point your eyes.

The list is hard to hear. Wars and commotions. Nation against nation. Earthquakes, famines, plagues. Arrests and betrayals, even by family. Jerusalem surrounded by armies. Signs in the sun, moon and stars, and the sea roaring. Yet threaded through it are calm sentences: "Be not terrified." "There shall not an hair of your head perish. In your patience possess ye your souls." Then the turn: "And then shall they see the Son of man coming in a cloud with power and great glory. And when these things begin to come to pass, then look up, and lift up your heads; for your redemption draweth nigh." When the news is terrible, the natural thing is to duck, to hunch, to stare at the ground. He tells them to stand up straight and look up. Redemption, apolytrosis, was a word for buying back a captive or a slave: release, coming toward you. Christians read this chapter in more than one way. Part of it, many say, came true within a generation: in the year seventy, Roman armies destroyed Jerusalem and its temple. Part of it, most Christians say, still waits for the day Christ returns. Some read nearly all of it as fulfilled; others nearly all as future. Some have tried to pull dates out of it, but the chapter never gives one. It gives a posture: when the world shakes, lift your head.
screen: `THE YEAR SEVENTY, AND THE DAY TO COME.`
then, large: `LOOK UP, AND LIFT UP YOUR HEADS.`

segments.voice: Notice your posture right now; if you've been scrolling, your head is probably bent and your shoulders curled. Breathe out, lift your chin a little, let your shoulders drop back, and look up at the ceiling or out at the sky for a few breaths. Hold one thing that frightens you with your head up instead of down, and if you pray, bring it to God from there.
Apolytrosis, Greek for redemption, release by a ransom paid: not duck and hide, but stand straight and look up.
Your line: your redemption draws near. Release, coming toward you, not away. Day five hundred seventy-five.

576.title: Watch and pray (Luke 21:29–38)
576.hook: don't let your hearts be weighed down with cares; watch and pray
576.howItsDone: Some Christians keep an evening prayer, such as Compline, to hand over the day before sleep, and some churches read this chapter in the season of Advent.

segments.voice: Yesterday, apolytrosis: when the world shakes, lift up your heads. Your line was your redemption draws near.

Jesus has been saying hard things about the end: wars, signs, Jerusalem surrounded by armies. His closing words aren't about armies at all. They're about a fig tree in leaf, and the weight a person carries all day and takes to bed at night. The unanswered email. The bill. The thing a sister said at dinner. Eleven at night, the day is over, and the mind is still running. His warning reads as if it were written for that hour.

First the tree. When the fig tree and all the trees put out leaves, you know summer is near. Nobody needs a calendar; you just look. Then a sentence about what lasts: "Heaven and earth shall pass away: but my words shall not pass away." And the warning, in the King James words: "Take heed to yourselves, lest at any time your hearts be overcharged with surfeiting, and drunkenness, and cares of this life, and so that day come upon you unawares." Overcharged: the Greek means weighed down, made heavy. Three things on the list. Surfeiting: the Greek word is used for the heavy head after a night of drinking, something close to a hangover. Drunkenness. And cares of this life: ordinary worries. He puts worry on the same list as a hangover; both leave the heart too heavy to notice what's coming. Then the cure: "Watch ye therefore, and pray always." The Greek for watch means to stay awake, like a guard on night duty. Not anxious. Alert. Luke ends the chapter with Jesus living it out. By day he teaches in the temple. Every night he goes out to spend the night on the Mount of Olives. Early every morning, the people come to hear him. Not a slogan for a crisis, but a rhythm: carry the day lightly enough that you can still see the leaves.
screen: then, large: `WATCH YE THEREFORE, AND PRAY ALWAYS.`

segments.voice: Notice what's sitting heaviest on you today and name it plainly, in a few words. Imagine it as an actual weight in your hands, and without solving anything, set it down for tonight on the floor beside the bed; it will still be there in the morning if you need it. If you pray, hand it to God by name.
Surfeiting, the heavy, hungover feeling Jesus warns can weigh a heart down, along with drunkenness and ordinary cares.
Your line: carry the day lightly enough. The fig tree is already in leaf. That's day five hundred seventy-six.

577.title: The room prepared (Luke 22:1–13)
577.hook: Satan enters Judas; a man with a water jar leads to an upper room
577.howItsDone: Christians remember the upper room on Maundy Thursday, the evening before Good Friday, and some congregations share a simple meal or set a table that night to recall it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, surfeiting, a heart weighed down, and a fig tree in leaf. Your line was carry the day lightly enough.

Two scenes, running at once in the same city. In the first, the city is filling up for Passover, the feast of unleavened bread, and the chief priests and scribes are looking for a way to take Jesus quietly, because they fear the crowds. One of the twelve slips away to meet them. In the second, two friends walk through crowded streets with strange directions: look for a man carrying a jar of water, and follow him home. One door opens to darkness. The other opens to a guest.
screen: `FOLLOW A MAN WITH A WATER JAR.`

segments.voice: Luke says it in one line, in the King James words: "Then entered Satan into Judas surnamed Iscariot, being of the number of the twelve." Not an outsider. One of the twelve Jesus had chosen by name. Judas goes to the chief priests and the temple captains, and they're glad, and agree to give him money. Luke doesn't explain why. People have guessed ever since: money, disappointment, politics. The text doesn't settle it, and it's honest to say so. Now the other scene. Jesus sends Peter and John to get the Passover ready: "there shall a man meet you, bearing a pitcher of water; follow him into the house where he entereth in." Some readers suggest carrying water was more often women's work, so a man with a jar may have stood out, an easy sign to follow. They're to ask the owner where the guest room is. "And he shall shew you a large upper room furnished: there make ready." The owner is never named. His room is simply furnished and ready for whoever the teacher sends. Peter and John find everything as they were told, and make ready the Passover. Two doors. One opened for betrayal, quietly, for a price. One opened for a meal, quietly, with no price named. The second, a stranger's spare room, is where Jesus will sit down to the Passover with his friends.
screen: `A MAN WITH A JAR STANDS OUT.`

segments.voice: Think of a space you have, even a small one, a spare chair, a corner of the kitchen table, and picture someone who could use a place to sit: a neighbor, a coworker eating alone. Picture getting it ready for them, clearing the chair, putting out a glass of water, turning on the light, without inviting anyone yet. If you pray, ask God to send whoever needs it.
Upper room, a stranger's large room, furnished and ready, where Jesus would keep the Passover with his friends.
Your line: make ready. The room was furnished before they arrived. Day five hundred seventy-seven, done.

578.title: With desire I have desired (Luke 22:14–23)
578.hook: he longed to eat this Passover with them, and gives bread and cup
578.tomorrow: I am among you as one who serves
578.howItsDone: Christians keep the Lord's Supper, also called Communion, the Eucharist or the Divine Liturgy, in weekly or even daily worship in some churches and monthly or quarterly in others, repeating Jesus's words over the bread and cup.

segments.voice: Yesterday, an upper room, furnished and waiting. Your line was make ready.

The room is ready. The hour has come. And Luke slows down. Before the bread, before the cup, before any of the words churches still repeat, Jesus says something personal. A dinner with someone not seen in years, a holiday table after a long time away: there's a kind of wanting that arrives before the food does. Jesus sits down with the twelve, and the first thing he tells them is how much he has wanted this evening.

In the King James words: "With desire I have desired to eat this passover with you before I suffer." Some readers hear in that doubling a Hebrew way of speaking carried into Greek: very much, with all of me. I have longed and longed. He knows what's coming, and wants to be at this table anyway. Then something that can surprise a first-time reader: Luke has two cups. First Jesus takes a cup, gives thanks, and tells them to share it. Then he takes bread, gives thanks, breaks it, and gives it to them: "This is my body which is given for you: this do in remembrance of me." After supper, another cup: "This cup is the new testament in my blood, which is shed for you." Jewish tradition describes several cups through the Passover meal, though no one can say exactly how it ran in Jesus' day. Remembrance, in Greek, is anamnesis. Some Christians hear more than memory in it: the past brought into the present. Christians understand the meal in different ways, and it's fair to say each plainly. Catholic and Orthodox Christians believe the bread and wine become the body and blood of Christ. Lutherans and many Anglicans speak of Christ truly present in the bread and wine. Many other Protestants keep the meal as a holy memorial and a sign. Each of them keeps it, because he asked. And then the hard line: the hand of the one who betrays him is on the table. They start asking each other who it could be.
screen: then, large: `WITH DESIRE I HAVE DESIRED.`

segments.voice: Think of someone you've been meaning to eat with and haven't, too busy, too far, too awkward, and picture the table: what you'd serve, where they'd sit. Imagine telling them at the start, before the food, that you've been looking forward to this; not a speech, just the truth. If you pray, give thanks for them by name.
Anamnesis, Greek for remembrance, do this in remembrance of me: a memory some hear as the past brought into the present.
Your line: I have longed for this. He said it first, before the bread. See you tomorrow.

579.title: I am among you as one who serves (Luke 22:24–38)
579.hook: at the table they argue who's greatest, and he tells Peter: I prayed for you
579.howItsDone: Churches that have deacons take the title from the same family of Greek words Jesus uses here for serving, and Christians pray for one another by name, especially for people facing a hard test.

segments.voice: Yesterday, anamnesis: remembrance that brings the past into the present, at a table Jesus longed for. Your line: I have longed for this.

The room might have gone silent. Jesus has just given them bread and said it's his body. He's just said one of them will betray him. And what happens next, Luke tells us without softening it, is an argument. Over dinner. About which of them is the greatest. It's almost funny, and painfully familiar: the meeting where everyone angles for credit, the family dinner where old rankings come back out. The friends at this table are doing exactly what people do.

Jesus doesn't shout. He asks a question. Kings lord it over people, he says, and get called benefactors. Not so with you. Then, in the King James words: "For whether is greater, he that sitteth at meat, or he that serveth? is not he that sitteth at meat? but I am among you as he that serveth." Everyone knows the answer: the one at the table outranks the one carrying the plates. And Jesus says, I'm the one carrying the plates. The Greek word for serving is the root of the word deacon. Then he turns to Peter, and his voice changes. "Simon, Simon, behold, Satan hath desired to have you, that he may sift you as wheat." The King James keeps a detail modern English can't show: in the Greek, that first you is plural. All of you will be shaken like grain in a sieve. Then the next line goes singular, just to Peter: "But I have prayed for thee, that thy faith fail not: and when thou art converted, strengthen thy brethren." Peter protests that he's ready to go to prison and to death. Jesus tells him that before the rooster crows today, he will deny three times that he knows him. Hear the order. The prayer comes before the failure. Jesus already knows Peter will fall, he has already prayed, and he's already given him a job for afterward: when you've come back, strengthen the others.
screen: `KINGS LORD IT; NOT SO WITH YOU.`
`I PRAYED FOR YOU, BEFORE YOU FELL.`
then, large: `I HAVE PRAYED FOR THEE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone heading into something hard, a test, a recovery, a marriage under strain, someone who might not make it through cleanly, and don't rehearse their mistakes. If you pray, do what Jesus did: pray for them now, ahead of time, that their faith won't fail. If you don't, hold them in good will, and decide now how you'll treat them if they stumble.
Deacon. The word rooted in Jesus's claim that at his table, he is the one who serves, carrying the plates instead of sitting to be served.
Your line: I have prayed for you. First the prayer, then the fall, then the way back. Until next time.

580.title: Sweat like drops of blood (Luke 22:39–46)
580.hook: on the Mount of Olives an angel strengthens him
580.howItsDone: Christians remember the agony in the garden on Maundy Thursday night, often by keeping watch in prayer for an hour, and Catholics pray it as the first sorrowful mystery of the rosary.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the word behind deacon: Jesus at the table as the one who serves, and a prayer for Peter before he fell. Your line: I have prayed for you.

After the supper, Luke says, Jesus went out to the Mount of Olives, as he usually did. This is his place; he's been sleeping out here all week. The disciples follow him in the dark, and he tells them to pray that they don't enter into temptation. Then he walks away from them, about a stone's throw, and kneels down. Close enough to hear, far enough to be alone. If you've ever stepped out of a hospital waiting room to stand in a hallway by yourself, you know that distance.

He prays, in the King James words: "Father, if thou be willing, remove this cup from me: nevertheless not my will, but thine, be done." The cup, in the Hebrew Bible, can be a picture of suffering poured out. He asks, honestly, not to drink it, then hands the answer back. Then two verses only Luke has. "And there appeared an angel unto him from heaven, strengthening him." The angel doesn't take the cup away, and doesn't explain anything. It gives him strength to go through. "And being in an agony he prayed more earnestly: and his sweat was as it were great drops of blood falling down to the ground." As it were: Luke is making a comparison. Some readers take it literally, pointing to a rare condition where extreme stress can bring blood into sweat. Others read it as a picture of how heavy the sweat fell. The text allows both. Agony, in Greek, was first a word for a contest, a wrestling match. Here he's wrestling in prayer. One honest note: these two verses are missing from some of the oldest manuscripts of Luke, and present in others. Scholars still debate whether they were original, and Christians have read and loved them for many centuries. When he gets up, he finds the disciples asleep, and Luke gently gives the reason: they were sleeping for sorrow.
screen: then, large: `AN ANGEL UNTO HIM, STRENGTHENING HIM.`

segments.voice: Think of one hard thing you can't avoid: a conversation, a diagnosis, a long week, a grief. Say honestly that you wish it would go away; Jesus said it too. Then shift the ask from take this from me to help me go through it, and if you pray, ask God for that strength; if you don't, notice where your own strength is, in your breath, your feet, the people near you.

Agonia, the Greek word for a struggle, an athlete's strain, the source of agony: Luke's picture of Jesus's prayer on the Mount of Olives, when he asked for the cup to pass and an angel came to strengthen him.

581.title: He touched his ear (Luke 22:47–53)
581.hook: a disciple strikes a servant with a sword; Jesus heals the man's ear
581.howItsDone: Christians remember the arrest during Holy Week, and some churches, such as the historic peace churches, return to scenes like this one when they teach about nonviolence.

segments.voice: Yesterday, agonia: a prayer wrestled out on the Mount of Olives, and an angel bringing strength. Your line: an angel strengthened him.

Night on the Mount of Olives. Jesus is still speaking when a crowd arrives, and walking in front of them is Judas. He comes close to kiss Jesus, and Jesus asks him quietly, in the King James words: "Judas, betrayest thou the Son of man with a kiss?" The disciples see what's happening. Someone asks, Lord, shall we strike with the sword? Before anyone answers, one of them swings. The blade catches the high priest's servant and cuts off his right ear. Blood on the ground, swords drawn in the dark, and everything about to get worse.

Then Jesus speaks. The King James has: "Suffer ye thus far." The Greek is just a few words, and translators aren't sure how to put them: let them have their way, or no more of this, enough. Either way, it's a word to stop. Then a detail only Luke tells: "And he touched his ear, and healed him." Jesus is being arrested. His friends are panicking. A night of trials and beatings is ahead. And in the middle of his own arrest, he heals a man from the side that came to take him: not one of his own, but a servant on the other side, bleeding in the dark. John's Gospel adds two names: the swordsman was Peter, and the servant was Malchus. Luke leaves them unnamed, and the scene works either way. Then Jesus turns to the chief priests, temple captains and elders who came out. You came with swords and clubs, as if I were a robber. I was with you every day in the temple, and you didn't lift a hand. "But this is your hour, and the power of darkness." Christians have gone back to this scene when they argue about violence and faith. Some hear in it a call to refuse force entirely; others hear a limit on it. Both start from what Jesus did with his hands.
